# Campaign targeting: a call list that survives a rate shock

Ranks bank customers by likelihood to open a term deposit, evaluated the way it would actually be
used: trained on past calls, scored on future ones.

**Data:** [Bank Marketing](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/222/bank+marketing) (UCI, Portuguese
bank, May 2008 to Nov 2010), `bank-additional-full.csv`, 41,188 calls.

## Why the evaluation setup matters

| Setup | AUC |
|---|---|
| Random split, with call duration | 0.955 |
| Random split, no duration | 0.815 |
| Chronological split, trained once on the first 80% | 0.670 |
| **Walk-forward: retrained before each of 5 test blocks** | **0.757** |

![Evaluation setups](figures/evaluation.png)

`duration` is only known after the call ends, so it can't be used to decide whom to call. The last 20%
of calls converted at 30.8% against 6.4% before, while the 3-month Euribor fell from 4.3% to 1.0%.
A model trained once never saw that regime; monthly retraining recovers most of the lost accuracy.

## Model comparison (same test rows) | Model | AUC trained once | AUC walk-forward | PR-AUC walk-forward | |---|---|---|---| | Logistic regression | 0.748 | 0.745 | 0.532 | | **Gradient boosting** | 0.670 | **0.757** | **0.585** | | Gradient boosting, client features only | 0.689 | 0.726 | 0.561 | ## What the list buys | Call the top | Share of subscribers reached | Conversion | Calls per sale | |---|---|---|---| | 10% | 24.0% | 74.0% | 1.35 | | 20% | 40.5% | 62.4% | 1.60 | | 30% | 53.5% | 55.0% | 1.82 | | Everyone | 100% | 30.8% | 3.24 |

Probabilities are still too low in the test period (mean prediction 21.5% vs 30.8% actual), so a production version would recalibrate each month on the latest outcomes before using scores as rates.

## Run
```bash
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
./download_data.sh
python train.py # writes results.json
python figures.py # writes figures/*.png
```

# Credit default risk: who should collections call first?

Predicts next-month default for 30,000 credit-card accounts and ranks them for an early-collections
team that can contact 20% of the book each month.

**Data:** [Default of Credit Card Clients](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/350/default+of+credit+card+clients)
(UCI, Taiwan 2005). 22.1% default rate.

## Results (30% stratified hold-out, 9,000 accounts) | Model | CV AUC | Test AUC | Gini | KS | Brier | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Logistic regression (scorecard baseline) | 0.761 | 0.754 | 0.508 | 0.399 | 0.142 | | Gradient boosting | 0.786 | **0.780** | 0.560 | 0.420 | 0.135 | At 20% contact capacity: | Ranking | Defaulted balance captured | Defaulters captured | Hit rate | |---|---|---|---| | **Model: expected loss (PD × balance)** | **77.4%** | 34.6% | 38.2% | | Model: PD only | 51.1% | 50.8% | 56.2% | | Rule: paid late last month | 54.0% | 47.3% | 52.3% | ![Capture curve](figures/capture_curve.png) Ranking by expected loss rather than probability alone is the main decision: it trades some hit rate for far more money at risk reached per call.

## Method
- Features: repayment status history, balances, payments, plus engineered utilisation, payment ratio,
months late, max delay and balance trend.
- `SEX` and `MARRIAGE` are excluded from the model. `SEX` is used only for a post-hoc audit: flag rates
20.6% (male) vs 19.6% (female) against actual default rates of 23.9% vs 21.0%; recall 0.33 vs 0.36.
- 5-fold stratified CV on the training set; permutation importance on the hold-out.

## Run
```bash
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
./download_data.sh
python train.py # writes results.json
python figures.py # writes figures/*.png
```

## Limits
Exposure is the latest statement balance, a proxy for exposure at default. Data is from 2005 Taiwan,
so the fitted model is a method demonstration, not a deployable scorecard.

# E-commerce clickstream: 110M events, from raw logs to a targeting model

Two months of behaviour from a large multi-category online store: **109,950,743 events** (views,
cart adds, purchases) from **5.3M users** in **23.0M sessions**, with **$505M** of purchases.
The questions are a product or growth team's: where does the funnel leak, what converts, do new
visitors come back, and who is about to buy?

**Data:** [eCommerce behavior data from multi category store](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mkechinov/ecommerce-behavior-data-from-multi-category-store)
(REES46, Oct–Nov 2019) on Kaggle, 14.7 GB of CSV. DuckDB converts it to 2 GB of Parquet and runs
every query over all rows on an 8 GB laptop.

## Headline results

| | |
|---|---|
| Cart abandonment | **59.4%** of sessions with a cart add end without a purchase (1.38M sessions) |
| Repeat buyers | **30%** of the 697,470 buyers bought on 2+ days, and they bring **66%** of revenue |
| Smartphones | **66%** of revenue ($335M). Samsung sells more phones than Apple (305k vs 243k), Apple earns 2.7× the revenue |
| Return visits | 15–27% of each weekly cohort of new visitors is active again the following week (lowest for the post-sale cohort) |
| Targeting model | Top 10% of users by predicted propensity contain **41.7%** of next-fortnight buyers, vs 36.8% for the best simple rule; AUC **0.796** vs 0.761 |

![Daily revenue and users](figures/daily.png)

![Daily revenue and users](figures/daily.png) **Data-quality finding.** On 15 November the log has 5.7M views and zero purchases, then the mid-November sale produces $23M and $58M on the 16th and 17th against a typical $7M day. That day is kept visible rather than smoothed over, and it matters for reading the model's test window.

Electronics sessions add to cart most often (13.4%) and convert best (8.0%); apparel converts at 2.2%. Once something is in the cart, 55–70% of carted sessions buy in every category. ![Purchases by weekday and hour](figures/hour_weekday.png) Purchases concentrate between 04:00 and 17:00 UTC. The Saturday and Sunday peaks are partly the 16–17 November sale weekend.

## Who buys in the next 15 days? A customer-level model evaluated on a later time window than it was trained on: | | Behaviour window | Label: bought in | Users | Buy rate | |---|---|---|---|---| | Train | 1–31 Oct | 1–15 Nov | 3,022,290 | 3.8% | | Test | 16 Oct–15 Nov | 16–30 Nov | 3,393,482 | 6.0% | | Method | AUC | Buyers in top 5% | Buyers in top 10% | Hit rate, top 10% | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Gradient boosting** | **0.796** | **26.7%** | **41.7%** | **25.1%** | | Rule: bought before | 0.761 | 23.3% | 32.9% | 19.8% | | Rule: carted in the last 7 days | 0.711 | 22.0% | 36.8% | 22.1% | | Rule: most recently active | 0.717 | 19.0% | 33.4% | 20.1% |
Past purchases, recency and breadth of products browsed carry most of the signal. The test fortnight includes the sale, so buy rates are higher than in training; the ranking still holds.

## Method
1. `ingest.py`: DuckDB reads each monthly CSV as text, parses timestamps, splits the top-level category
and writes ZSTD Parquet (42.4M October rows, 67.5M November rows).
2. `analyze.py`: session funnel, daily trend, weekday × hour, category and brand conversion, smartphone
price bands, weekly cohorts and repeat buyers, all in SQL over the full data.
3. `model.py`: 19 behavioural features per user (activity counts, sessions, active days, recency,
tenure, products and categories browsed, prices viewed and carted, spend, last-7-day and last-day
activity, category mix and top category). Negatives are down-sampled to 25% with matching weights for training;
the test set is scored in full.
4. `figures.py`: charts above.

## Run
```bash
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
./download_data.sh # needs ~/.kaggle/kaggle.json; ~4.6 GB download, 14.7 GB unpacked
python ingest.py # CSV -> Parquet (then the CSVs can be deleted)
python analyze.py # results/analysis.json
python model.py # results/model.json
python figures.py # figures/*.png
```

*Timestamps are UTC. Prices are as logged by the store. Sessions follow the dataset's own `user_session` id.*

# Entrata (ENT): equity initiation

**Constructive. Base target price $16.50 per share** (sensitivity range about $15–$18).

An initiation-style view of Entrata ahead of its IPO, built from the S-1/A: a units × ARPU revenue
build, a linked three-statement model, and a relative valuation against vertical-SaaS peers.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`Entrata_ENT_Initiation.pdf`](Entrata_ENT_Initiation.pdf) | 10-page initiation report: thesis, assumptions, revenue build, KPIs, P&L, cash flow, comps, target price, risks |
| [`Entrata_ENT_Model.xlsx`](Entrata_ENT_Model.xlsx) | The model: Cover, Assumptions, Revenue Build, KPIs & Commentary, 3-Statement Model, Valuation, Sources |

## Thesis
- **Large, under-digitised market.** About $1T of annual rent across 23.4M U.S. multifamily units; Entrata
powers about 2.5M (roughly 10%).
- **Enterprise validation.** 233 customers above $500K ARR make up 84% of ARR.
- **Unified data and AI flywheel.** Property management, payments, resident experience and the ELI+ AI layer
on one data model raise switching costs and ARPU without needing new units.

## Model
| $M | 2024A | 2025A | 2026E | 2027E | 2028E |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 412 | 509 | 612 | 720 | 832 |
| Growth | – | 24% | 20% | 18% | 16% |
| Gross margin | 56% | 60% | 62% | 63% | 64% |
| Non-GAAP operating margin | 14% | 23% | 26% | 28% | 30% |
| Adjusted FCF margin | 2% | 16% | 17% | 19% | 20% |

Revenue = units × ARPU. Units grow 11% → 10% → 9% as the base scales; ARPU grows 8% → 7% → 6% on
cross-sell, payments and ELI+, reaching $256 in 2028E against a ~$580 benchmark for high-ARPU customers.

## Valuation
| Method | Multiple | Price / share | Weight |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026E EV / Revenue | 5.7× | $16.15 | 50% |
| 2027E EV / Revenue, discounted one year | 5.5× | $16.71 | 30% |
| 2026E EV / Non-GAAP operating income | 22× | $16.21 | 20% |
| **Weighted** (less $270M net debt, 199.2M diluted shares) | | **$16.33 → $16.50** | |

The 5.7× multiple is a premium to the 4.7× median of the selected vertical-SaaS set (AppFolio, CoStar,
Procore, Guidewire, Tyler, ServiceTitan), supported by 117% net retention, a Rule of 40 near 47% and the
enterprise mix. Horizontal and HCM SaaS names (Monday.com, BILL, Paycom, Paylocity) are kept as a cross-check only.

## Risks to monitor
- Gross retention slipping from 99% to 97%.
- Lumpy embedded-payments and transaction revenue.
- Final IPO share count, dilution and the controlled-company structure.

*Public-market data was taken at the time of writing and moves daily. Not investment advice.*

# Lending Club: which loans should an investor buy?

An end-to-end analysis of **2,260,668 funded loans ($34.0B) and 27,648,741 rejected applications**
from Lending Club, 2007–2018. The question is an investor's: does the extra interest on riskier loans
pay for the extra losses, and can a model trained on older loans pick better new ones than
Lending Club's own grades?

**Data:** [Lending Club loan data](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/wordsforthewise/lending-club) on
Kaggle, about 3.5 GB of CSV. DuckDB streams it into Parquet and runs every aggregate out of core, so
the whole pipeline fits in 8 GB of RAM.

## Headline results

| Buying 2015 36-month loans (283,026 loans, never seen in training) | Realised return | Charge-off rate |
|---|---|---|
| Every loan | 2.14% a year | 14.9% |
| Grade A only | 2.25% | 5.4% |
| Highest interest rates, top 20% | 1.49% | 26.9% |
| Lowest predicted default, top 20% | 2.40% | 4.2% |
| **Highest predicted return, top 20%** | **2.91%** | 13.9% |
| **Highest predicted return, top 10%** | **3.16%** | 14.0% |

- **Chasing yield loses money.** Grades E, F and G charge 19–27% interest but their 2015 loans realised 0.7%, −0.6% and −1.8% a year.
- **The model adds about 0.8 points a year** over buying the whole book, with a default rate no higher than average.
- **Inside every grade, the safer half pays more.** Dropping the riskier half by predicted default lifts
grade D from 1.61% to 2.29% and grade E from 0.72% to 1.69%.

![Strategies](figures/strategies.png)

## What the data shows

![Volume and approval](figures/volume_approval.png)

Volume grew from $0.02B in 2008 to $7.9B in 2018 while applications grew faster: the approval rate
peaked at 15.1% in 2013 and fell to 5.0% in 2018. Among 2016–2018 applications, approval falls from
about 11% at a 15–20% debt-to-income ratio to under 1% above 40%.

![Vintage heatmap](figures/vintage_heatmap.png)

Loss rates by grade were stable from 2009 to 2013, then rose for C–G loans issued in 2014 and 2015,
the years volume grew fastest. Grade F charged off 27% of 2013 loans and 42% of 2015 loans.

![Sub-grade economics](figures/subgrade_economics.png)

Interest rates rise in a straight line across sub-grades; losses rise faster. Realised return peaks
around B4 (3.1% a year) and falls away below grade D.
## Method

1. **Ingest** (`ingest.py`): DuckDB reads the gzipped CSVs as text, casts 34 useful columns (rates,
dates such as `Dec-2015`, employment length) and writes ZSTD Parquet. 30M rows in a few minutes.
2. **Only count finished loans.** The snapshot ends in December 2018, so a loan's outcome is only final
once its term has run: 36-month loans issued up to 2015 and 60-month loans up to 2013. That leaves
676,302 resolved loans; counting still-running loans as "good" would understate losses badly.
3. **Analyse** (`analyze.py`): approval rates, grade mix, vintage curves, sub-grade economics, purpose and FICO bands, all in SQL.
4. **Model** (`model.py`): gradient boosting on what an investor sees at issuance only: loan terms,
income, DTI, FICO, credit history, purpose, state, and Lending Club's grade and rate. Anything

income, DTI, FICO, credit history, purpose, state, and Lending Club's grade and rate. Anything
recorded after issuance (payments, recoveries, last FICO) is excluded. Trained on 393,276 loans
issued 2007–2014; tested on 283,026 36-month loans issued in 2015.
- A default classifier (AUC and importance) and a return regressor (for picking loans).
5. **Figures** (`figures.py`).

| Default model, 2015 test loans | AUC | |---|---| | Lending Club sub-grade alone | 0.679 | | Model without Lending Club's grade or rate | 0.676 | | Model with grade and rate | **0.696** | Borrower data alone matches Lending Club's own grading; combining both is best. The model under-predicts 2015 defaults slightly (29.2% predicted vs 32.4% observed in the riskiest decile), consistent with the worse 2015 vintage above.

## Definitions and limits
- **Realised return** = (total cash received ÷ amount funded)^(1/3) − 1 for 36-month loans, pooled
dollar-weighted. It ignores reinvesting early repayments, so it understates true IRR for every
strategy equally; the comparisons between strategies are the point.
- **Charge-off** includes `Charged Off`, `Default` and the older "does not meet the credit policy" charge-offs.
- Fees and taxes are not modelled. Past Lending Club performance says nothing about any current product.

## Run
```bash
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
./download_data.sh # needs ~/.kaggle/kaggle.json
python ingest.py # CSV -> Parquet
python analyze.py # results/analysis.json
python model.py # results/model.json
python figures.py # figures/*.png
```

Currency Conversion Approach: Converting Budget and
Actuals into INR
While reviewing the dashboard, I identified that the Actual and Budget values were available
in multiple currencies such as INR, GBP, and USD. Since adding different currencies directly
would give an incorrect consolidated number, I converted both Actuals and Budget into one
reporting currency: INR.
1. FX Rate Table Preparation
I used the FX_Rates table as the source for currency conversion. Since the FX table had
multiple daily rates for the same currency, I first standardized it before linking it to the financial
data.
The key preparation steps were:
• Cleaned the Currency column by trimming spaces and keeping a consistent currency
code format.
• Converted the date field into a proper date format.
• Created a MonthStart column from the FX date so that daily rates could be aligned
with monthly Actual and Budget data.

• Created a MonthStart column from the FX date so that daily rates could be aligned
with monthly Actual and Budget data.
• Grouped the FX table by MonthStart and Currency.
• Took the average FX rate for each currency-month combination.
• Created a clean monthly FX table named FX_Rates_Monthly_Avg.
The grouping logic was:
MonthStart + Currency
This helped create one average FX rate for each currency in each month.
For example:
MonthStart Currency Avg Rate to INR
Apr-2026 USD Average USD to INR rate for Apr-2026
Apr-2026 GBP Average GBP to INR rate for Apr-2026
Apr-2026 INR 1
This ensured that every monthly Budget and Actual value could be converted using the correct
monthly average rate.

2. Creation of FX Key
To link the FX rate table with Actuals and Budget, I created a common key called FX_Key.
The FX_Key was created using:
Currency + MonthStart
Example:
USD|2026-04-01
This key was created in all three relevant tables:
• FX_Rates_Monthly_Avg
• Fact_Budget
• Fact_Actuals
The logic was:
FX_Key = Currency & "|" & MonthStart
This allowed Power BI to correctly match each Actual and Budget row with the right currency
rate for that month.

3. Data Modelling
After creating the FX_Key, I linked the monthly FX table with the Actual and Budget fact tables.
The relationships used were:
FX_Rates_Monthly_Avg[FX_Key] → Fact_Budget[FX_Key]
FX_Rates_Monthly_Avg[FX_Key] → Fact_Actuals[FX_Key]
The relationship was set as:
• Many-To-One
• Single direction
• Active relationship
This means one monthly FX rate is applied to multiple Actual or Budget rows belonging to the
same currency and month.

4. Budget Conversion into INR
Once the FX relationship was created, I created a Budget INR measure.
Budget INR =
SUMX (
Fact_Budget,
Fact_Budget[BudgetAmount_num]
* RELATED ( FX_Rates_Monthly_Avg[Avg_RateToINR_Accounting] )
)
This measure works row by row. It takes each Budget amount, finds the matching monthly FX
rate using the relationship, converts it into INR, and then sums all converted values.
For example:
• INR budget is multiplied by 1
• USD budget is multiplied by USD to INR rate
• GBP budget is multiplied by GBP to INR rate
This gives one consolidated Budget value in INR.

5. Actual Conversion into INR
Similarly, I converted Actuals into INR using the same FX logic.
Actual INR =
SUMX (
Fact_Actuals,
Fact_Actuals[Amount_num]
* RELATED ( FX_Rates_Monthly_Avg[Avg_RateToINR_Accounting] )
)
This ensures that Actuals are also converted into INR using the same monthly average FX rate
logic.
This step was important because Actual and Budget should be compared in the same reporting
currency. Comparing Actual in local currency with Budget in INR would give an incorrect
variance.

6. INR-Based Variance Measures
After converting both Actual and Budget into INR, I created INR-based variance measures.
Variance INR =
[Actual INR] - [Budget INR]
Variance % INR =
DIVIDE ( [Variance INR], [Budget INR] )

This gives a like-for-like comparison because both sides are now in INR.
For this OPEX dashboard:
• Positive variance means Actual INR is higher than Budget INR, which indicates
overspend.
• Negative variance means Actual INR is lower than Budget INR, which indicates saving.

7. Dashboard Update
After creating INR-based measures, I updated the Executive Summary dashboard to use the
converted INR measures.
The KPI cards were updated to:
• Actual INR
• Budget INR
• Variance INR
• Variance % INR
I also updated the monthly trend and variance visuals to use INR-based measures instead of
the original local currency measures.
This made the dashboard more accurate because it now compares all values in one reporting
currency.

8. Final Result
The final model now converts INR, USD, and GBP values into INR before aggregation. This
avoids incorrect summing of mixed currencies and gives a proper consolidated view of Actual,
Budget, Variance, and Variance %.
The key logic used was:
• Average FX rate at currency-month level
• Common FX_Key using Currency + MonthStart
• Relationship between FX table and fact tables
• INR conversion using row-level multiplication through SUMX
• Final KPI and variance measures based on INR values

# Pulse — case study

*From "system of record" to "system of action": a next-best-action engine for STORM.*

## 1. Context

STORM is the RM platform — CRM, analytics, transactions, and an AI agent working alongside the RM.
An RM's day, as I understand it from the outside:

- A book of 30–50 HNI/UHNI families, ₹250–500 Cr under advice.
- Capacity for roughly ten meaningful conversations a day, on a good day.
- Inbound decides the day: the client who calls, the AIF that's closing, the CA who wants a statement.
- The CRM records what happened. It doesn't say what should happen next.

The constraint is not product knowledge or effort. It is **attention allocation**: 40 clients, 10 slots,
and the ten are chosen by recency of noise rather than by value or urgency.

## 2. The problem I chose

The JD says the job is to "find what's broken or underperforming, fix it, make it measurably better",
and that PMs here build before they write. So I built the thing I'd want to demo in my first month:
a Morning Brief that answers, for each RM, *who do I call today and why* — and the diagnostics that
justify it.

I chose STORM over the client app because the leverage is higher: one RM decision moves ₹ crores;
and because the same signal engine can later power the client app's insight cards, which is how I'd
extend it (see §7).

## 3. What the data says

I generated a realistic synthetic book (240 clients, ₹2,150 Cr, 6 RMs; see `docs/DATA_MODEL.md`) and
asked it the six questions I'd ask STORM's warehouse in week one. Numbers below are from that book —
they demonstrate the mechanism; the *queries* (`app/analytics.py`) are the deliverable.

| # | Finding | Number |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | AUM that hasn't heard from an RM in 60+ days | **12.9% — ₹277 Cr, 46 clients** |
| 2 | MF onboarding completion; where it leaks | **56% complete; 27% of those who reach the bank e-mandate stall there** |
| 3 | Cash idle for 6+ weeks | **₹82 Cr across 33 clients** → ~₹3.1 Cr/yr client drag, ~₹66 L/yr fee revenue |
| 4 | Repeat in-app product interest with no logged RM conversation | **87% (33 of 38 client-product pairs)** |
| 5 | Redemptions preceded by withdraw-screen views | **10 of 17 in 60 days; 15 had no RM contact in the prior 3 weeks** |
| 6 | Open signals vs daily capacity, per RM | **59–85 signals vs 10 conversations/day** |

The pattern: the data already knows. The app logs intent, the ledger shows idle money, the CRM shows
silence. None of it reaches the RM as a *decision*.

## 4. Hypothesis

> If each RM starts the day with a ranked, explained, rupee-quantified list of clients to contact,
> then coverage of at-risk AUM and conversion of observed intent will rise — because the bottleneck is
> attention allocation, not product knowledge.

Falsifiable: if RMs ignore the list (action rate < 30%) or the list's conversion is no better than the
RM's own picks (shadow-mode baseline), the hypothesis is wrong and the engine should be shut off.

## 5. What I built, and the decisions inside it

**Signals as SQL, not a model.** Thirteen questions, one file each, over the warehouse tables. Why:
explainable (an RM can argue with a threshold; nobody argues with a score), auditable (compliance can
read it), portable (it runs on STORM's Postgres/BigQuery unchanged), and fast to iterate. A model
comes later, trained on the outcomes this collects.

**Score = ₹ in play × conversion prior × urgency.** Every signal has to say how much money it is
about, how likely a conversation is to move it, and how time-bound it is. Summed per client, this gives
one number to rank on. The priors are stated assumptions (`app/engine.py`) — the product's job is to
replace them with measured rates.

**Suitability gates live in the SQL.** Buy-intent and product-closing never surface a PMS to a client
without ₹50 L of headroom or an AIF to a Conservative profile. Compliance by construction, not by RM
judgement under time pressure.

**Ten a day, not all of them.** The brief shows the top 10. Everything else is one click away. Alert
fatigue is the default failure mode of these tools; capacity is the design constraint.

**A feedback loop from day one.** Done / Snooze / Not relevant (with a reason) on every row. "Not
relevant" rates per signal type are the calibration signal: above 20%, the threshold is wrong.

**The AI writes the brief, not the decision.** Claude gets a minimal, identifier-free 360 and returns
a structured brief: talking points with evidence, a WhatsApp draft, objections, compliance checks,
phrases to avoid. The ranking stays deterministic and inspectable; the language model does what it's
good at — synthesis and tone. If the API is unavailable, a template brief renders; the RM is never
blocked.

**Ask STORM shows its SQL.** A natural-language question becomes a query through a read-only tool,
and the RM sees both the answer and the SQL — trust through transparency, and the query is reusable.

**One engine, two surfaces.** Seven of the thirteen signals have a client-facing version (idle cash,
maturity, SIP mandate, drift, overlap, concentration, tax harvest). Retention and intent signals are
RM-only. The Client 360 shows both renderings side by side.

## 6. How we'd know it works

- **North star:** incremental net flows from signal-led conversations (₹/month); AUM retained on churn
signals as the second headline.
- **Primary:** action rate (signals acted on within 48h, target ≥ 60%); conversion rate (acted →
outcome within 14 days).
- **Leading:** time-to-first-contact on urgency ≥ 0.8 signals (< 24h); % of AUM contacted in the
trailing 30 days.
- **Guardrails:** opt-outs/complaints per 100 contacts; suitability exceptions (must be zero); "not
relevant" rate per signal type (< 20%); RM time per actioned signal; redemption rate in treatment.

**Experiment.** Client-level randomisation *within* each RM's book, 50/50, six weeks. RM skill is the
largest confounder; randomising clients inside each book controls for it and gives every RM the tool.
Contamination (an RM applying a learning to a control client) biases toward the null — acceptable.
With ~240 clients the pilot is powered for large effects on flows only, so the readout leans on action
and conversion rates by signal type, and on the shadow-mode baseline.

## 7. Rollout

1. **Week 0–1, shadow mode.** Compute signals, show nobody. Measure what RMs would have done anyway.
2. **Week 2–7, pilot.** Morning Brief live for treatment clients. Weekly readout. A signal with a
"not relevant" rate above 20% gets fixed or switched off that week.
3. **Week 8, readout and recalibration.** Priors re-fit from outcomes; thresholds tuned.
4. **Week 9+, client app.** The same `signals` table powers insight cards for self-serve segments,
starting with idle cash and SIP mandate (lowest risk, highest volume).

## 8. Risks

- **Alert fatigue** — mitigated by the cap, the feedback loop, and killing bad signals fast.
- **RM trust** — mitigated by showing evidence and SQL, never a black-box score.
- **Data quality** — stale ledger balances or unlogged calls create false positives; the "not relevant"
reasons make data gaps visible to leadership instead of silently eroding trust.
- **Privacy / DPDP** — client data reaches the LLM only for the brief, minimal and identifier-free;
production needs a VPC deployment, retention controls and audit logs per brief.
- **Compliance** — no return promises anywhere in prompts or templates; suitability gates in SQL; the
brief lists the checks the RM must do before acting.

## 10. What I learned building it

- Realistic synthetic data is a product exercise in itself: deciding base rates forced me to think
about what "normal" looks like for an HNI book before deciding what "broken" is.
- The hardest product decisions were about *silence*: when a signal should not fire (mid-onboarding,
already discussed, unsuitable). Most of the SQL is exclusions.
- Structured output turns an LLM into a component: the UI never parses prose, and the fallback is a
first-class path rather than an error state.

# Pulse — a next-best-action engine for wealth RMs

> **Every morning, the ten clients your RM should call — and why.**
> A working prototype built for the Associate Product Manager role at Ionic Wealth, aimed at the
> STORM job description line: *"an AI agent working alongside the RM"*.

An RM with 40 HNI clients can have about ten real conversations a day. Today those ten are chosen by
whoever called last. Pulse chooses them from the data: **thirteen SQL-defined signals**, each with a
rupee amount, an urgency and a conversion prior, ranked into a Morning Brief — with a Claude-written
call brief one click away, a natural-language SQL agent for the RM's own questions, and a
"what's broken" analytics page that shows the diagnosis before the cure.

```

(stand-in for │ (13 questions, (scored: │
```

- **Python 3.12 · FastAPI · DuckDB · Jinja2 · Anthropic SDK.** No build step, no JS framework, one process.

directly), keep the SQL, publish `signals` daily. The Morning Brief becomes a STORM widget; the client
app reads the same table for insight cards.
- The generator (`scripts/generate_data.py`) plants every story at a realistic base rate — idle cash 18%,
churn 8%, buy intent 9%, stuck onboarding 3.5% … — so the engine has true things to find and plenty
of clients where it should stay quiet. Schema: [docs/DATA_MODEL.md](docs/DATA_MODEL.md).

# Rolling revenue forecast: a 4-week reforecast, backtested

Forecasts daily revenue 28 days ahead for a UK online giftware wholesaler, the way an FP&A team
reforecasts at each month start, and checks every method against nine real month-starts in 2011.

**Data:** [Online Retail II](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/502/online+retail+ii) (UCI),
1,067,371 invoice lines, Dec 2009 to Dec 2011. Cancellations, returns, zero prices and non-product
lines (postage, fees, manual adjustments) removed before aggregating to daily revenue.

![Weekly revenue](figures/weekly_revenue.png)

## Backtest (origins: 1st of each month, Mar to Nov 2011)

| Method | Daily WAPE | Avg. miss on 4-week total | Bias | Worst month |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Recent 4-week weekday average | 32.9% | 14.6% | −7.6% | −31.0% |
| Last year + growth | 34.1% | 10.2% | +0.5% | −22.1% |
| Gradient boosting | 32.5% | 11.4% | −1.0% | −37.7% |
| **Blend: boosting + last year** | **31.6%** | **9.4%** | **−0.3%** | −29.9% |

![November reforecast](figures/november_forecast.png)

![November reforecast](figures/november_forecast.png)

- Daily error is high because a handful of large wholesale orders swing single days; the 4-week total
is the number a finance team plans against.
- The boosting model predicts each day as a multiple of the trailing 28-day level, using weekday,
season, days to Christmas and last year's shape, trained on every past origin before the forecast date.
- 10th to 90th percentile intervals from quantile boosting cover 73.6% of open days against an 80% target,
so they run slightly narrow.
